request.system:
You are assisting with the qualitative analysis of interview data from a study of frontline hotel employees' work experiences. You will receive one passage from an interview transcript. Code the passage as a qualitative researcher would in first-order coding, and complete the coding form below.

About the passage
- The passage begins with brief details about the interviewee: role, gender and years in the job.
- Lines marked "Interviewer:" are the interviewer's questions. Lines marked "Interviewee:" are the interviewee's answers.
- Some passages contain two excerpts from the same interview, marked [Earlier in the interview] and [Later in the interview].

The coding form
1. codes: Give between 3 and 6 first-order codes. Each code has a short label of 2 to 6 words, kept close to the interviewee's own language, and one supporting quote. Each quote must be copied word for word from the passage, without any change, and must be no longer than 30 words.
2. interpretation: In one or two sentences, in your own words, state what the interviewee is communicating in this passage.
3. tone: The overall tone of the interviewee's account. Choose one: positive, negative, mixed or neutral.
4. confidence: An integer from 0 to 100 indicating how confident you are that your interpretation is accurate.

Respond only with a JSON object that follows the schema provided. Write in English.
request.user:
Interviewee details: Room attendant, female, 2nd year

Interviewer: Is there anything at work that’s made a particularly strong impression on you?

Interviewee: Last month a guest phoned after checking out to say a gold bracelet had gone missing from the bedside table, and I was the one who’d cleaned that room. A colleague from Security came over and asked me questions for a few minutes, what time I went into the room and what time I came out, then had a look at my cleaning trolley as the procedure requires. It took about ten minutes altogether. He was very polite about it, and even told me it was just routine and not to worry. Once he was done, he let me go back to cleaning rooms. It didn’t hold anything up. I said I’d cooperate, that it was only right, the hotel has rules, anyone would have to be checked. The next day the guest found it herself, in the inner pocket of her make-up bag. The lobby manager phoned to let me know, and I said it’s fine, I’m glad it’s been found. The guest was quite embarrassed about it. Before checking out she made a point of leaving a box of walnut shortbread from her hometown for me at the front desk, with a little card that said, sorry for the trouble. I took it to the staff canteen at lunchtime and shared it with my colleagues, and everyone joked that next time something like this happens, I should get the guest to bring a couple more boxes. Now when I clean a room, I do it the same as before, leaving the door half open as the standard says and hanging up the cleaning sign. Later my team leader mentioned it at a meeting. She said it had been handled well, Security and Housekeeping had worked well together, and this is the procedure we should follow from now on. Around that time my mum phoned and asked how work was going. I said it’s fine, and told her about the shortbread. She laughed for ages and said the guests at our hotel have very good manners.
